Title: DisasterInsight: A Multimodal Benchmark for Function-Aware and Grounded Disaster Assessment
Abstract Summary: Introduces DisasterInsight, restructuring xBD into ~112K building-centered instances with instruction-diverse evaluation across building-function classification, damage-level/disaster-type classification, counting, and structured report generation. Proposes DI-Chat (LoRA fine-tuned baseline) which improves damage/disaster-type classification and report generation, while building-function classification remains hard for all models.
Study design: Benchmark dataset introduction + baseline model paper
Primary task(s): Building Function Classification (BFC); Damage Level Classification (DLC); Disaster Type Classification (DTC); Building Counting (BC); Structured Report Generation (SRG)
Disaster type(s)\/domain: Multi-hazard: 19 disaster events, 5 hazard types (tsunami, earthquake, flooding, fire, hurricane) from xBD
Modalities used: RGB optical, bi-temporal (pre/post-disaster) imagery; bounding boxes; OSM-derived metadata; text
Dataset(s) introduced (new): DisasterInsight (built on xBD with OSM building-function annotations)
Dataset size: 112,507 building-centered instances; 270,096 total instruction-following instances (202,837 train / 67,259 eval)
Model\/architecture(s) evaluated: LLaVA-OneVision, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-8B, Qwen3-VL-30B, TeoChat, DI-Chat (TeoChat), DI-Chat (Qwen2.5-VL-7B)
Fine-tuning method: LoRA — (r,α)=(64,128) for TeoChat and (32,64) for Qwen2.5-VL-7B; applied to language model only, frozen vision backbone
Fusion strategy: Video-LLaVA-style multimodal training; shared MLP projection layer; scene-level summarization pipeline aggregates per-building metadata (function/damage/location) for scene-level tasks
Missing-modality\/sensor-gap handling: Not reported (single sensor, RGB optical only)
Class-imbalance reporting\/handling: Measured/reported only — Fig. 2(c) shows severe imbalance (e.g., residential 74,549 vs. government_emergency 134); no correction method described
Evaluation metric type: Classical classification metrics (macro-F1, accuracy, ordinal MAE) + classical NLP metrics (BLEU-4, ROUGE-L, BERTScore F1) + MAE/RMSE (counting). No rubric/LLM-judge or human-rated metrics.
Primary result\/headline metric + value: DI-Chat (TeoChat): avg F1 46.36%, avg accuracy 87.76%, DLC ordinal MAE 0.220, BLEU 18.45, ROUGE-L 35.85, BERTScore 88.03; DI-Chat (Qwen2.5-VL-7B): avg F1 46.13%, BERTScore 89.45%
Ground-truth human verification process: Ground-truth reports generated by Llama 3.3 70B Instruct (selected after comparing hallucination/grounding across candidate LLMs); paper states OSM labels are used 'rather than authoritative or exhaustive ground truth' but no explicit human audit/verification process is described for reports
Output\/evaluation human review process: Not reported (evaluation is fully automatic — F1, BLEU, ROUGE-L, BERTScore, MAE)
Reporting of limitations: Yes — Section 5 states limitations: noisy OSM-derived function labels, reliance on optical imagery only, automatically generated (unverified) reports
Identified research gap: Existing RS datasets (xBD, BRIGHT, FloodNet) treat buildings as an undifferentiated class and lack function-aware, instance-level evaluation and structured reporting aligned with humanitarian assessment practices (INSARAG/FEMA)
Future work directions: Multimodal extensions, improved annotations, expert human evaluation (stated in Discussion/Limitations)
Key contribution: First building-centered, function-aware, multi-task disaster VLM benchmark (112,507 instances, 5 tasks) with OSM-derived function labels and a structured report-generation task aligned to humanitarian guidelines
Relevance to HARBOR\/PILOT: High — builds on xBD and uses LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-VL (same model family as HARBOR/PILOT's Qwen2-VL-7B); its documented building-function-classification failure and severe class imbalance (Fig. 2c) directly validates HARBOR/PILOT's stratified disaster×severity balancing rationale.

Year: Received 22 Dec 2025; Accepted 12 Jan 2026; Published 13 Jan 2026 (Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 818)
Title: EdgeV-SE: Self-Reflective Fine-Tuning Framework for Edge-Deployable Vision-Language Models
Abstract Summary: Proposes EdgeV-SE, a self-reflective fine-tuning framework with asymmetric dual pathways (generative linguistic + discriminative visual) that estimates uncertainty via log-likelihood margin and refines decisions via consistency regularization and cross-pathway mutual learning, without any inference-time overhead. Tested on hurricane damage assessment; improves classification accuracy, image-text alignment, and caption quality while preserving latency/memory on NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano.
Study design: Method paper (novel fine-tuning framework) + ablation study + on-device benchmark
Primary task(s): Binary image classification (damage vs. no-damage) + image captioning
Deployment setting: Edge — target hardware NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano (satellite IoT / communication-denied disaster environments)
Modalities used: RGB optical satellite images + generated text captions
Dataset(s) introduced (new): None explicitly introduced as new — dataset is a curated/filtered/relabeled subset of an existing Kaggle dataset with authors' own pseudo-caption generation and manual audit
Dataset(s) reused (existing): 'Satellite Images of Hurricane Damage' (Kaggle, Mader) [46]; Wildfire Prediction Dataset (Kaggle, Aaba, Canadian Open Government Portal) [52]
Dataset size: Hurricane: 14,000 images total (5,000/5,000 train; 1,000/1,000 val; 1,000/1,000 test); Wildfire: identical balanced structure, 14,000 images total
Model\/architecture(s) evaluated: Salesforce/blip-image-captioning-large (BLIP-Large); LLaVA-1.5-7B used only as offline pseudo-caption annotator
Fine-tuning method: QLoRA (r=16, α=32, dropout=0.05) on selected text layers + last 2 ViT blocks for EdgeV-SE and comparison methods; Standard SFT baseline uses text-only LoRA (r=128, α=256)
Fusion strategy: Asymmetric dual-pathway architecture — generative linguistic pathway (text-decoder class-verbalizer log-likelihoods) + auxiliary discriminative visual pathway (lightweight MLP head on frozen vision-encoder features); combined via margin-based consistency regularization + Jensen-Shannon-divergence mutual learning
Class-imbalance reporting\/handling: Handled via dataset construction — explicitly balanced 5,000/5,000 train and 1,000/1,000 val/test per class rather than corrected post-hoc
Domain\/distribution-shift handling: Addressed directly — Section 5.9 tests hurricane→wildfire domain generalization with identical pipeline/hyperparameters (no retuning); Section 5.6 tests robustness under 7 image corruptions × 5 severities (rotation, brightness, contrast, blur, noise, JPEG, occlusion)
Explainability\/interpretability method: Log-likelihood margin (Δ) between class verbalizers reported as an interpretable decision-confidence signal (Section 5.4); qualitative side-by-side comparisons vs. baseline
Uncertainty\/calibration approach: Explicit — temperature scaling (grid search T∈{0.5,...,3.0}; optimal T=2.0 via validation ECE minimization); Expected Calibration Error (15 bins); 95% bootstrap CIs (1000 resamples); reliability diagrams
Evaluation metric type: Classical classification metrics (Accuracy, class-wise F1, Macro-F1, ECE) + classical captioning metrics (CIDEr-D, BERTScore, CLIPScore) + human-rated (100-sample human-verified hallucination study, Section 5.8, 2 annotators, inter-annotator agreement reported)
Baseline(s) compared against: Standard SFT, Controlled SFT, Self-Rewarding VLM, Iterative Self-Correction
Primary result\/headline metric + value: Macro-F1 improved from 0.911 (Standard SFT) to 0.985 (EdgeV-SE); test-set ECE = 3.2% [95% CI 2.7–3.6]; CIDEr-D 38.37, BERTScore 90.82, CLIPScore 28.21
Real-world\/on-device deployment evidenc: Yes — extensive: NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano (8GB), 15W MAXN, FP16, batch=1; EdgeV-SE latency 1837.2 ms/image, throughput 0.544 FPS, peak memory 0.915 GB — identical to Controlled SFT baseline, confirming zero added inference overhead
Ground-truth human verification process: Yes — manual audit of ~200 randomly sampled pseudo-captions (LLaVA-1.5-7B generated); ~8% judged noisy and excluded pre-split; inter-annotator agreement >90%
Output\/evaluation human review process: Yes — separate 100-sample human-verified hallucination study on final model outputs (Section 5.8): 2 independent annotators, balanced 50/50 damage/no-damage, 3-level severity taxonomy, agreement 92–94%, Wilson 95% CIs reported
Reporting of limitations: Yes — Section 6.5: pseudo-ground-truth reliance, single-domain focus (mitigated by wildfire test), single backbone (BLIP-Large only), single hardware target (no Raspberry Pi/Coral), no lightweight-classifier baseline comparison
Identified research gap: Standard SFT is data-inefficient/insufficient for robustness under scarce labels and visually subtle damage cues; existing self-correction methods rely on inference-time iterative prompting (added latency), unsuitable for edge deployment; few works exploit disentangled linguistic/visual pathways for self-reflective tuning
Future work directions: Human-verified multi-hazard benchmark (hurricanes, floods, wildfires, earthquakes) with structured damage attributes; continual/active learning using low-margin samples flagged for human review; deployment-aware optimization (quantization, pruning, distillation) across lighter VLM backbones
Key contribution: Training-time self-reflective fine-tuning framework using uncertainty-weighted consistency + mutual learning between dual pathways, achieving substantial accuracy/calibration/caption-quality gains with zero inference-time overhead, validated on real edge hardware
Relevance to HARBOR\/PILOT: Very High — closest architectural/methodological analog to HARBOR/PILOT: parameter-efficient fine-tuning of a similarly-scaled VLM on disaster imagery, explicit ECE/calibration reporting, and a rigorous two-stage human-verification protocol (ground-truth audit + separate output-hallucination study) that directly models what HARBOR/PILOT's reviewer-validation GUI should formalize.

Title: Efficient Few-Shot Learning in Remote Sensing: Fusing Vision and Vision-Language Models
Abstract Summary: Investigates combining vision models (YOLOv8) and VLMs (LLaVA, ChatGPT, Gemini) for aircraft detection and scene understanding in remote sensing, evaluated on labelled/unlabelled and degraded imagery. Reports average MAE improvement of 48.46% in aircraft counting and 6.17% improvement in CLIPScore when bounding boxes augment VLM prompts.
Study design: Empirical pipeline/system paper (integration of existing detector + existing VLMs; no VLM fine-tuning)
Primary task(s): Visual Question Answering (aircraft counting); VQA (disaster route-obstruction assessment); visual captioning
Disaster type(s)\/domain: Aircraft detection (primary domain); disaster-response satellite imagery used qualitatively for secondary investigation (specific disaster type not stated in text)
Deployment setting: Not specified as an operational target; YOLOv8s inference run on NVIDIA A100 GPU; VLM inference via local (LLaVA) or API-based (ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Flash) queries
Modalities used: RGB optical imagery (satellite/aerial) + text (VQA prompts/answers, captions) + bounding-box annotations
Dataset(s) reused (existing): Airbus Aircraft Detection Dataset [22]; disaster satellite imagery dataset (Hajkova/EU Space Imaging) [23]
Dataset size: Airbus Aircraft Detection Dataset: 103 high-resolution images; disaster dataset size Not reported (used qualitatively only)
Model\/architecture(s) evaluated: YOLOv8s (fine-tuned) + LLaVA v1.5-13B-3GB, ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Flash (all VLMs used zero-shot)
Fine-tuning method: None — zero-shot/prompting only for VLMs; only YOLOv8s detector fine-tuned (50 epochs, batch 16, 512×512, pretrained weights, cosine LR schedule from 0.01)
Fusion strategy: Detection-first pre-processing pipeline — YOLOv8s bounding boxes passed as visual/textual context within VLM prompts (region-proposal-style fusion) rather than joint training or raw-image-only prompting
Missing-modality\/sensor-gap handling: Not reported (single optical sensor; robustness tested via synthetic Gaussian noise degradation, not sensor/modality gap)
Class-imbalance reporting\/handling: Not reported (single-class detection task — aircraft only)
Domain\/distribution-shift handling: Partially addressed — tested under 'degraded' images (Gaussian noise, mean=0, std=50) vs. raw images to simulate real-world conditions
Explainability\/interpretability method: Not reported as a dedicated method (bounding boxes function as a visual grounding aid for VLM reasoning, not framed as explainability)
Evaluation metric type: Classical metrics (MAE for counting, CLIPScore for image-text alignment) + human-rated (manual evaluation of description accuracy/relevance, Tables 4–8)
Baseline(s) compared against: Raw-image VLM prompting (no bounding boxes) vs. raw+bounding-box prompting; also raw vs. degraded conditions
Primary result\/headline metric + value: Average MAE improvement of 48.46% across models (counting, raw+degraded combined) when bounding boxes added; average CLIPScore improvement of 6.17% across models
Real-world\/on-device deployment evidenc: Partial — runtime benchmarked (YOLOv8s ~12ms/image on A100; VLM ~300ms/box LLaVA local, ~0.9s Gemini API, ~1.2s ChatGPT-4o API; total pipeline ~1.0–1.5s to ~3–6s) but not on edge/mobile hardware
Ground-truth human verification process: Not reported (no VLM fine-tuning; YOLOv8s trained on pre-existing dataset annotations)
Output\/evaluation human review process: Yes — manual evaluation of VLM-generated descriptions/answers explicitly conducted (Section 5.2, Tables 4–8), including on the secondary disaster/evacuation-route dataset
Reporting of limitations: Limited — no dedicated limitations section; notes CLIPScore 'may not reliably measure conceptual alignment in degraded images' and that LLaVA 'may not fully capitalize on additional context... even in optimal conditions'
Identified research gap: VLM applications to remote sensing remain underexplored given their generalist nature; traditional vision models require extensive domain-specific labelled data and lack contextual understanding; detection+VLM integration has not been systematically applied across distinct RS domains (structured counting vs. unstructured disaster interpretation)
Future work directions: Not extensively detailed; states methodology is 'task-agnostic and can be extended to other domains, including land cover classification and change detection, with minimal architectural modifications'
Key contribution: Demonstrates that fusing a fine-tuned object detector (YOLOv8) with zero-shot VLMs via bounding-box-augmented prompting substantially improves counting accuracy and descriptive/contextual quality without any VLM fine-tuning, including under degraded conditions
Relevance to HARBOR\/PILOT: Moderate — useful contrast/ablation reference (detection-guided zero-shot prompting vs. HARBOR/PILOT's full QLoRA fine-tuning) supporting the argument that fine-tuning is needed for structured, damage-specific rescue guidance; does not directly inform QLoRA, xBD, or RAR design choices.

Title: Harnessing Large Language Models for Disaster Management: A Survey
Abstract Summary: Presents the first systematic survey of LLM applications in disaster management, introducing a taxonomy across four disaster phases (mitigation, preparedness, response, recovery) and three LLM architecture types. Compiles public datasets and identifies challenges (dataset construction, efficient deployment, robust generation, unified evaluation) and opportunities for LLM-driven disaster management.
Primary task(s): Meta-review spanning classification, estimation, extraction, and generation tasks (vulnerability classification, occurrence classification, warning/plan generation, relevance/situation/information/need classification, location/summary extraction, report generation, damage classification/estimation, sentiment classification)
Disaster type(s)\/domain: All-hazard, natural disasters primarily (man-made disasters explicitly excluded per Limitations), organized across 4 phases: Mitigation, Preparedness, Response, Recovery
Deployment setting: Not specified (survey; individual cited works vary and are not consistently reported)
Modalities used: Text (social media, news — predominant); image (satellite/social media imagery in some cited works); multimodal combinations vary by cited study
No. of modalities: Varies by cited work — survey categorizes into Encoder-based LLM (ELM), (Encoder-)Decoder LLM (DLM), Multimodal LLM (MLLM)
Dataset(s) introduced (new): None — survey introduces no new dataset
Dataset(s) reused (existing): Compiles 26+ existing datasets (Appendix B Table 2), incl. CrisisLexT6/T26, CrisisNLP, SWDM2013, ISCRAM2013, DRD, DSM, AIDR, CrisisMMD, Multi-Crisis, CrisisBench, Eyewitness Messages, TREC Incident Streams, HumAID, EPIC, DYFI, FloodDepth, Behavioral Facilitation, DisasterMM, Ré-SoCIO, CrisisFACTS, DisasterQA, FFD-IQA, FloodNet
Dataset size: Not applicable as a single figure; per-dataset sizes tabulated in Appendix B (e.g., CrisisLexT6 = 60,082 samples; HumAID = 77,000 tweets; CrisisMMD = 16,058 tweet+image pairs)
Model\/architecture(s) evaluated: Not applicable (survey does not itself evaluate models); categorizes cited works' models as encoder-based (e.g., BERT), (encoder-)decoder (e.g., GPT), or multimodal LLM
Fine-tuning method: Not applicable; notes fine-tuning and prompting as the two commonly employed techniques across surveyed works generally, without specifying ranks/parameters
Fusion strategy: Not applicable; notes multimodal fusion strategies used across cited works include simple feature aggregation, attention-based/cross-attention mechanisms, dual transformer architectures, Cycle-GAN with mixed fusion
Class-imbalance reporting\/handling: Discussed as an open 'Dataset Construction' challenge — raw disaster data 'often contains uncertainty and bias'; synthetic data generation proposed as a mitigation direction (Section 5)
Domain\/distribution-shift handling: Discussed as an open challenge — e.g., Multi-Crisis dataset cited for evaluating transfer learning from high-resource to low-resource languages and unseen crisis domains (Section 4)
Explainability\/interpretability method: Rationale extraction (evidence supporting classification decisions) noted as used in some surveyed works, e.g. RACLC (Section 3.3.3)
Uncertainty\/calibration approach: Mentioned only as a future-direction mitigation strategy for hallucination ('uncertainty estimation', citing Xu et al., Section 5) — not a finding of the survey itself
Evaluation metric type: Classical metrics reported across surveyed works: accuracy, F1 (classification); MAE (estimation); BLEU (generation/summarization); token-level classification metrics (extraction)
Primary result\/headline metric + value: Not applicable (survey); reports that surveyed papers are heavily concentrated on the Response phase (Fig. 3 pie chart shows values of 72.4%/13.4%/12.6%/1.6% across the four phases; exact phase-to-percentage mapping not explicitly stated in text beyond the chart)
Reporting of limitations: Yes — explicit Limitations section: survey scope excludes non-LLM applications and man-made disasters; categorization based on model architecture only (not size/efficiency/performance); only accessible/open-sourced datasets included
Identified research gap: Most studies deploy generic LLMs as universal solutions without domain-specific tailored frameworks; applications heavily concentrated on the Response phase, other phases underexplored; datasets skewed toward classification tasks; explicitly flags lack of a unified evaluation protocol for generative tasks (report/summary generation) since annotation criteria differ across datasets, making published results difficult to compare directly
Future work directions: Innovative dataset construction (synthetic data generation) for broader disaster-scenario coverage; efficient deployment balancing lightweight models with robustness; robust generation via RAG, domain-specific training, uncertainty estimation to reduce hallucination; building a unified evaluation protocol for reliable comparisons
Key contribution: First systematic review of LLM applications across all four disaster-management phases; novel taxonomy integrating application scenarios, specific tasks, and model architectures; compiled resource list of public datasets and identified key challenges/future directions
Relevance to HARBOR\/PILOT: High — supplies the taxonomy language (mitigation/preparedness/response/recovery) for positioning HARBOR/PILOT within the Response phase, and explicitly names the 'unified evaluation protocol' gap for generative disaster tasks as an open challenge — directly justifying the need for a standardized rubric-based metric like RAR.

Title: DisasterM3: A Remote Sensing Vision-Language Dataset for Disaster Damage Assessment and Response
Abstract Summary: Curates DisasterM3, the first remote sensing VLM dataset for global-scale disaster assessment: 26,988 bi-temporal satellite images and 123k instruction pairs across 5 continents, spanning 36 events / 10 disaster types, multi-sensor (optical+SAR), and 9 tasks. Benchmarks 14 VLMs (finding SOTA models struggle) and fine-tunes 4 models, achieving up to 10.4% QA, 2.1-point Report, and 40.8% Referring-Segmentation gains with cross-sensor/cross-disaster generalization.
Study design: Benchmark dataset introduction + fine-tuning/method paper (NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks track)
Primary task(s): 9 tasks: disaster type recognition, disaster scene recognition, disaster-bearing-body recognition, damaged building counting, damaged road area estimation, damage segmentation, referring segmentation, damaged object relational reasoning, disaster comprehensive report (caption + restoration advice)
Disaster type(s)\/domain: Multi-hazard: 36 historical events across 5 continents, 10 types (fire, tornado, earthquake, explosion, tsunami, volcano, hurricane, flooding, landslide, conflict)
Deployment setting: Not specified as edge/cloud/satellite IoT; framed as supporting 'rescue teams and planning personnel' with no stated hardware deployment target
Modalities used: RGB optical (pre- and post-disaster) + Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR, post-disaster only) + text (instructions, QA, captions, segmentation masks)
No. of modalities: 3 (optical imagery, SAR imagery, text) — optical-optical and optical-SAR pairings both evaluated
Dataset(s) reused (existing): xBD [9], BRIGHT [5] (26 of 36 events); Maxar Open Data program (10 new events); Capella Space and Umbra (SAR sources); AID dataset [47] (13 land-use categories reused)
Dataset size: 26,988 bi-temporal images (22,214 optical, 4,774 SAR); 123,010 instruction pairs total; Instruct set: 17,190 optical / 3,798 SAR / 92,968 pairs; Bench set: 5,024 optical / 976 SAR / 30,042 pairs; 15,881 multi-temporal pairs
Model\/architecture(s) evaluated: LLaVA-1.5-7B, LLaVA-OneVision-7B, Kimi-VL-A3B-Instruct/Think, InternVL3 (8B/14B/78B), Qwen2.5-VL (3B/7B/32B/72B), GeoChat-7B, TeoChat-7B, EarthDial-4B, GPT-4o, GPT-4.1 (QA); LISA-7B, PSALM-1.3B, HyperSeg-3B, GeoPixel-7B (referring segmentation) — 14 VLMs benchmarked total
Fine-tuning method: Fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-8B, LISA, and PSALM on the DisasterM3 Instruct set; exact LoRA/QLoRA rank/alpha values Not reported in main text (deferred to Appendix §B, not present in provided excerpt)
Fusion strategy: Bi-temporal (pre/post-disaster) paired image input; optical-optical and optical-SAR settings evaluated separately; referring-segmentation models compared on mask-token design (PSALM's Mask2Former-style multiple mask tokens vs. LISA's single fixed mask token)
Missing-modality\/sensor-gap handling: Core focus — explicitly quantifies the optical-SAR cross-sensor performance gap (Section 4.1, Fig. 7); SAR shows 'reduced semantics... and underrepresentation in generic VLM' causing substantially diminished performance; fine-tuning partially (not fully) closes this gap
Class-imbalance reporting\/handling: Measured/reported only — Fig. 2 reports building damage ratio (intact 92.85%, damaged 5.34%, destroyed 1.81%) and road damage ratio (intact 79.44%, flooded 12.94%, debris 7.62%) as revealing 'actual challenges for model optimization'; no explicit correction/reweighting method described
Domain\/distribution-shift handling: Explicitly tested — cross-sensor (optical vs. SAR) and cross-disaster-category generalization (Table 4: accuracy varies by disaster type, e.g., landslide highest, earthquake/tornado/explosion lowest)
Explainability\/interpretability method: Not reported as a dedicated method (object relational reasoning and referring segmentation provide localized/grounded outputs functioning as a form of interpretability)
Evaluation metric type: Classical classification metrics (Accuracy %) for multiple-choice tasks; rubric-based/LLM-as-judge — open-ended tasks (caption, restoration advice) scored by GPT-4.1 on a 5-point scale across sub-dimensions (damage assessment precision, damage detail recall, factual correctness; recovery necessity, strategic completeness, action priority precision); mIoU/cIoU for referring segmentation. No human-rated evaluation of model outputs.
Baseline(s) compared against: 14 zero-shot pretrained VLMs (open-source, remote-sensing-specific, commercial) vs. 4 fine-tuned models; Random Guess baseline for multiple-choice accuracy
Primary result\/headline metric + value: Fine-tuning gains up to 10.4% (QA accuracy, InternVL3-8B avg), 2.1 points (Report score), 40.8% (Referring Segmentation mIoU, PSALM-1.3B); e.g., PSALM-1.3B optical-optical mIoU improves 9.7%→50.5% after fine-tuning
Real-world\/on-device deployment evidenc: Not reported — experiments run on 4 NVIDIA H100 GPUs (96GB) for training/testing (per NeurIPS checklist), not edge/deployment hardware
Ground-truth human verification process: Yes — multi-round human verification pipeline (Fig. 6): disaster domain experts annotate correct answers for GPT-4o-generated question variants (recognition), annotate bounding boxes/relationship descriptions (reasoning), and multiple experts draft captions/restoration advice per UNITAR/FEMA guidelines before GPT-4o polishing and multi-round human verification (further detail deferred to Appendix §A, not in provided excerpt)
Output\/evaluation human review process: Not reported for the benchmark evaluation itself — GPT-4.1 used as automated judge for open-ended tasks rather than human raters (Section 4, Evaluation Metrics)
Reporting of limitations: Yes — explicit Section 5 'Limitations and Future Directions': fixed 0.8m resolution limits multi-resolution generalization; SAR limited to single polarization; cross-sensor gap remains significant; counting-task overfitting observed (fine-tuned InternVL3-8B degrades outside low-density range, Section 4.2/Fig. 8)
Identified research gap: Mature RS vision-language datasets exist for general geospatial tasks, but none combine multi-hazard, multi-sensor, and multi-task (multi-granularity: recognition→counting→localization→reasoning→report) requirements in one benchmark; existing RS VLMs (GeoChat, TeoChat, EarthDial) transfer poorly to disaster-specific characteristics
Future work directions: Multi-resolution generalization (Sentinel-2/Landsat via geo-registration); enhanced sensor diversity (multi-polarization SAR, e.g. Sentinel-1 VV+VH); cross-sensor alignment strategies; counting-task optimization (object-sensitive encoders e.g. DINOv2, numerical-difference loss, diffusion-based synthetic data, knowledge distillation); maintaining DisasterM3 as a 'living benchmark' with new events added over time
Key contribution: First multi-hazard, multi-sensor (optical+SAR), multi-task (9 tasks) remote sensing VLM dataset (26,988 images, 123,010 instructions, 36 events, 10 disaster types); benchmarks 14 VLMs revealing systematic weaknesses; demonstrates fine-tuning yields consistent, robust cross-sensor/cross-disaster generalization gains
Relevance to HARBOR\/PILOT: Very High — near-identical scope to HARBOR/PILOT: fine-tunes Qwen2.5-VL (same model family as Qwen2-VL-7B) on xBD-derived disaster imagery for structured VLM tasks. Its documented counting-task overfitting (Section 4.2) directly parallels a risk in HARBOR/PILOT's building-count/RAR pipeline, and its GPT-4.1-as-judge rubric scoring for report/advice generation is a directly comparable design precedent for RAR's rubric-based evaluation approach.
